In my time, back in my own country, this money came from import duties. Citizens imagined foreign importers paid them, a comforting belief; in reality, Americans paid. The burden was distributed with such perfect equality that a man worth a hundred million dollars and a day laborer’s nursing baby each contributed exactly six dollars a year. You couldn’t ask for anything more equal, I suppose. Scotland and Ireland paid tribute to Arthur, and the British Islands together had just under a million inhabitants. A skilled worker earned an average of three cents a day when he covered his own living costs. On that basis, national government spending came to ninety thousand dollars a year, or roughly two hundred and fifty dollars daily. By handing out nickels instead of gold on a day devoted to curing the king’s evil, I therefore hurt nobody, disappointed nobody, pleased everyone involved, and saved four-fifths of that day’s national expenditure besides. In the America of my time, the equivalent saving would have been eight hundred thousand dollars. My substitution drew on wisdom from a very distant source: my boyhood. A true statesman never scorns wisdom, however humble its origins. As a boy, I always kept my pennies and gave buttons to foreign missions. Buttons would serve the ignorant savage just as well as coins, while coins served me better than buttons. Everyone was happy, and nobody suffered.

Marinel dealt with the patients as they arrived. He examined each applicant, sending away those who failed to qualify and passing the others on to the king. A priest recited, “They will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover.” While the reading continued, the king stroked the sores. Finally, the patient completed the ceremony, received his nickel—the king personally hung it around his neck—and was sent away. Would you expect that to cure anyone? It certainly did. Any ritual nonsense can cure a patient who believes in it strongly enough. Near Astolat stood a chapel where the Virgin had once appeared to a girl who tended geese nearby—the girl herself said so. They built the chapel on that spot and hung a picture of the event inside. You might have thought it dangerous for sick people to go near such a picture. Instead, thousands of sick and disabled people came every year, prayed before it, and departed perfectly healthy. Even healthy people could look at it and survive.

She would live among people who loved her and had better judgment than she did. Her life would be quiet enough to keep her safe and busy enough to keep her cheerful. No one would lead her into temptation or leave her alone for temptation to find her. She would be happy and respected. Emma admitted that Harriet was the luckiest person in the world to have inspired such steady, lasting love in such a man—or, if not quite the luckiest, second only to Emma herself.

Her commitments to the Martins naturally kept Harriet away from Hartfield more and more, and this was no cause for regret. She and Emma would have to become less close. Their friendship must settle into a calmer affection. Fortunately, this necessary change already seemed to be happening, gradually and naturally.

Before September ended, Emma went with Harriet to church and watched her marry Robert Martin with complete satisfaction. No memories, even those connected with Mr. Elton standing before them, could spoil her pleasure. Perhaps at that moment she scarcely thought of Mr. Elton as anything except the minister who might next bless her own marriage. Robert Martin and Harriet Smith, the last of the three couples to become engaged, were the first to marry.

Jane Fairfax had already left Highbury and returned to the comfort of her beloved home with the Campbells. The two Mr. Churchills were also in London, waiting only for November.

Emma and Mr. Knightley had settled, as far as they dared, on the month between. They had decided they should marry while John and Isabella were still at Hartfield. That would allow them to go away for the two-week seaside trip they planned. John and Isabella approved, as did all their other friends. But Mr. Woodhouse—how could they persuade him to agree? So far, he had spoken of their marriage only as something far in the future.

When they first raised the subject, it made him so miserable that they almost lost hope. Mentioning it a second time caused less distress. He began to think that the marriage would happen and that he could not prevent it, a promising step toward acceptance. Even so, he was unhappy. In fact, he looked so unhappy that his daughter lost her courage. She could not bear to watch him suffer and know he imagined himself neglected. Both Mr. Knightleys assured her that once the wedding was over, his distress would soon pass too. Her reason almost accepted this, but she hesitated. She could not go ahead.

Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall in Somersetshire never read for pleasure anything except the Baronetage. It occupied his idle hours and comforted his troubled ones. Its accounts of the few surviving titles from the earliest grants stirred his admiration and respect. Any unpleasant feelings caused by family affairs naturally gave way to pity and contempt as he browsed the almost endless titles created during the previous century. And if every other page failed him, the story of his own life always held his interest. His favorite book invariably opened at this entry:

“Elliot of Kellynch Hall.

“Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760; married July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq., of South Park, Gloucestershire. With her, who died in 1800, he had the following children: Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a stillborn son, November 5, 1789; Mary, born November 20, 1791.”

That was exactly how the printers had first produced the paragraph. Sir Walter, however, had improved it for his own and his family’s information by adding after Mary’s birth date: “Married December 16, 1810, Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq., of Uppercross, Somersetshire.” He had also inserted, with perfect accuracy, the day and month of his wife’s death.

Next came the customary account of the old and distinguished family’s origins and advancement: its first settlement in Cheshire; its mention in Dugdale; service as high sheriff; representation of a borough in three successive parliaments; displays of loyalty; and the baronetcy granted in the first year of Charles II’s reign. All the Marys and Elizabeths whom its members had married were included. Together these details filled two handsome pages of the small volume, ending with the coat of arms, the motto, and “Principal residence, Kellynch Hall, Somersetshire.” Sir Walter’s handwriting supplied one final addition:

“Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great-grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity defined Sir Walter Elliot from beginning to end: vanity about both his appearance and his position. Remarkably handsome when young, he remained a striking man at fifty-four. Few women cared more about their looks, and no newly created lord’s valet could take greater delight in his place in society. He ranked beauty second only to a baronetcy among life’s blessings. Sir Walter Elliot, possessing both, therefore received his own unwavering respect and devotion.

His good looks and rank did have one legitimate claim to his affection: they must have won him a wife whose character was far better than his own deserved.
